extracted.intended_audience: students and instructors of mathematical logic (advanced undergraduates / beginning graduate students)
extracted.subtask_description: Textbook material on (1) introducing defined function symbols and formal interpretations between theories (how to translate one language/theory into another) and (2) constructing and using a nonstandard model of the reals (*R) to treat infinitesimals, finite/infinitesimal elements, standard part, convergence, and differentiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper form of a definition of a function symbol (δ)
rubrics_metrics.description: A function symbol f not in the original language is introduced by a sentence of the form ∀v1 ∀v2[ f v1 = v2 ↔ ϕ ], where ϕ is a formula in the original language (i.e., not containing f) in which only v1 and v2 may occur free.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the canonical way to add a new function symbol by definition; the formula ϕ must not contain f and must use only the intended free variables so that the definition intends to name a unique object for each argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Noncreative definition ≡ well-definedness (Theorem 27A)
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) Noncreative: For any sentence σ in the smaller language, if T; δ |= σ (in the augmented language), then already T |= σ. (b) f is well defined: T contains the sentence ∀v1 ∃!v2 ϕ. These two conditions are equivalent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: a 'good' definition should not allow deriving new facts in the original language that were not already consequences of T. Example of a bad definition given: defining f by f(x)=y iff x<y which makes f(1)=2 and f(1)=3 producing contradiction. Proof sketch: δ implies ε, and conversely if T |= ε one can build the unique function F in each model A of T to extend A to a model of δ and preserve original-language sentences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation π: requirement for universe formula π∀
rubrics_metrics.description: An interpretation π of L0 into T1 assigns to the special parameter '∀' a formula π∀ of L1 in which at most v1 occurs free, such that T1 |= ∃v1 π∀.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intuition: π∀ should define a nonempty domain (universe) inside any model of T1 to serve as the universe of the interpreted L0-structure; the theory T1 must prove that the defining formula picks out at least one element.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation π: assignment for predicate symbols πP
rubrics_metrics.description: π assigns to each n-place predicate parameter P of L0 a formula πP of L1 in which at most variables v1,...,vn occur free, so that πP defines the interpreted relation on the universe specified by π∀.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: πP is used to interpret an n-ary predicate of L0 as an n-ary relation definable in T1; when forming πB, one restricts that relation to the set defined by π∀ in the model B of T1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation π: assignment for function symbols πf with uniqueness condition
rubrics_metrics.description: π assigns to each n-place function symbol f of L0 a formula πf of L1 in which at most v1,...,vn,vn+1 occur free, such that T1 |= ∀v1...∀vn(π∀(v1) → ... → π∀(vn) → ∃x(π∀(x) ∧ ∀vn+1(πf(v1,...,vn+1) ↔ vn+1 = x))).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This condition ensures that in any model of T1, πf defines a unique output in the set defined by π∀ for each tuple of inputs in that set (i.e., πf genuinely defines a function on the interpreted universe). The constant case (n=0) is the existence of a unique x satisfying πc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructing the interpreted structure πB and π^{-1}[T1]
rubrics_metrics.description: |πB| = set defined in B by π∀; relations P^{πB} are the relations defined by πP restricted to |πB|; functions f^{πB}(a1,...,an) = the unique b with |=B πf[[a1,...,an,b]]. Define π^{-1}[T1] = Th{πB | B ∈ Mod T1} = {σ | σ is an L0-sentence true in every πB obtainable from a model B of T1}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: π^{-1}[T1] is a theory in L0: sentences true in every structure obtained by applying π to models of T1. It is satisfiable iff T1 is satisfiable. This is the semantic effect of the syntactic interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faithful interpretation between theories
rubrics_metrics.description: An interpretation π of a theory T0 into a theory T1 is an interpretation π of the languages such that T0 ⊆ π^{-1}[T1], equivalently σ ∈ T0 ⇒ σ^π ∈ T1. If T0 = π^{-1}[T1], π is faithful and σ ∈ T0 ⇔ σ^π ∈ T1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Faithfulness means the interpreting theory T1 proves exactly the translations of the sentences of T0; examples include embedding (N;0,S) into (Z;+·) with appropriate π. Faithful interpretations allow transferring completeness/decidability/undecidability results between theories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Syntactical translation ϕ ↦ ϕ^π (recursive algorithm)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a formula ϕ of L0, define ϕ^π recursively: for an atomic formula scan right-to-left, replace the rightmost function-term segment g x1...xn by a fresh variable y and prefix ∀y(πg(x1,...,xn,y) → ...), continue until no function-symbols remain, and replace predicate P by πP; for connectives, (¬ϕ)^π = ¬(ϕ^π), (ϕ→ψ)^π = (ϕ^π → ψ^π), and (∀x ϕ)^π = ∀x(π∀(x) → ϕ^π) (quantifiers are relativized to π∀).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example given: (P f g x)^π = ∀y(πg(x,y) → ∀z(πf(y,z) → πP(z))). This is the concrete procedure for producing the L1-formula whose truth in B corresponds to truth of ϕ in πB.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correctness lemma for syntactical translation (Lemma 27B)
rubrics_metrics.description: For π an interpretation of L0 into T1 and B a model of T1, for any formula ϕ of L0 and any assignment s of variables into |πB|, |=_{πB} ϕ[s] iff |=_B ϕ^π[s].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by induction on formula complexity (atomic case uses induction on number of function-symbol occurrences). This lemma makes precise the claim that ϕ^π 'says the same thing' about B as ϕ says about πB.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eliminability of defined function symbols (Theorem 27D)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given T with ε := ∀v1 ∃!v2 ϕ and δ := ∀v1 ∀v2( f v1 = v2 ↔ ϕ ), and L+ the language with f added, then for any L+-sentence σ there is a sentence σ^π in the original language such that (a) T; δ |= (σ ↔ σ^π), (b) T; δ |= σ ⇔ T |= σ^π, and (c) if f does not occur in σ then |= (σ ↔ σ^π).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation π (identity except πf=ϕ) is faithful for Cn(T;δ) into T, so definitions of f are eliminable: any sentence about the extended language is equivalent (modulo T;δ) to one in the original language. This justifies conservative extension by properly formed definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method to construct a nonstandard real field (*R) via compactness
rubrics_metrics.description: Start with a sufficiently large first-order language containing a constant symbol c_r for each real r and predicate/function symbols for every relation/operation on R. Consider Th_R ∪ { c_r < v1 | r ∈ R } and apply compactness to obtain a model A and an element a satisfying all statements c_r < a, making a infinite; then embed R into A and arrange an isomorphic structure *R in which R is a substructure and *R ≡ R.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This yields a nonstandard model ∗R elementarily equivalent to R but containing infinite elements and infinitesimals; the construction exploits compactness by finitary satisfiability in R of finite subsets of the added set of sentences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transfer principle (expressible properties transfer to *R)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any property of R that can be expressed by a sentence of the chosen first-order language holds in *R as well (since R ≡ *R).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply to show ∗< is transitive, ∗+ is commutative, field axioms hold in ∗R, etc. Caution: properties not expressible in the language (e.g., completeness/least-upper-bound property) may fail in ∗R; the method applies only to first-order expressible statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions of finite elements F and infinitesimals I in *R
rubrics_metrics.description: F = { x ∈ ∗R | *|x| < y for some y ∈ R } and I = { x ∈ ∗R | *|x| < y for all positive y ∈ R }.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: F consists of elements bounded by some standard real, I consists of elements smaller than every positive standard real. Example: reciprocals of infinite elements are infinitesimals; 0 is the only standard infinitesimal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraic facts: F is a subring; I is an ideal (Theorem 28A)
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) F is closed under addition, subtraction, and multiplication. (b) I is closed under addition, subtraction, multiplication, and if x ∈ I and z ∈ F then x·z ∈ I.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Algebraic consequence: F is a subring of ∗R and I is an ideal in F; these facts are proved by transferring arithmetic inequalities expressible in the language and manipulating bounds using standard reals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infinitely-closeness relation (#) and its properties (Theorem 28B)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define x # y iff x - y ∈ I. Then # is an equivalence relation on ∗R; if u # v and x # y then u + x # v + y and -u # -v; if u # v and x # y and all are finite then u·x # v·y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This formalizes the idea of two elements being infinitesimally close. Use closure properties of I to verify algebraic compatibility of # with addition, negation, and multiplication (for finite elements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of a standard between infinitely close points when at least one is finite (Lemma 28C)
rubrics_metrics.description: If x # y and at least one of x,y is finite, then there is a standard q strictly between x and y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in proofs establishing uniqueness of the standard part; the lemma is proved by choosing a suitable standard bound b and using least m with x < m b to get an intervening standard multiple.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard part decomposition and uniqueness (Theorem 28D & Corollary 28E)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every x ∈ F (finite) is infinitely close to a unique r ∈ R (its least-upper-bound of standard reals below x). Thus every finite x decomposes uniquely as x = s + i where s is standard and i infinitesimal; define st(x)=s.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Algebraic viewpoint: st : F → R is a ring homomorphism with kernel I, so F/I ≅ R. The standard part map provides a bridge back to standard analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Properties of the standard part map st (Theorem 28F)
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) st maps F onto R. (b) st(x)=0 iff x is infinitesimal. (c) st(x + y) = st(x) + st(y). (d) st(x · y) = st(x) · st(y).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These properties follow from the fact st(x) # x and from algebraic properties of I and F; they make st a homomorphism from the ring F onto the real field with kernel I.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of convergence via infinitesimals and equivalence to ε–δ
rubrics_metrics.description: F : R → R converges at a to b iff whenever x is infinitely close to (but different from) a, then ∗F(x) is infinitely close to b. This is equivalent to the usual ε–δ definition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof of equivalence: formalize ε–δ sentences in the language and transfer to ∗R, and conversely use infinitesimal δ to witness the ε–δ condition. This provides a nonstandard characterization of limits and continuity (continuity iff x # a ⇒ ∗F(x) # F(a)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivative via infinitesimals and standard-part rule
rubrics_metrics.description: F'(a)=b iff for every nonzero infinitesimal dx, dF/dx # b where dF = ∗F(a + dx) − F(a). When derivative exists, F'(a) = st(dF/dx) for any nonzero infinitesimal dx.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This allows computing derivatives by algebraic manipulation of infinitesimals (e.g., (a+dx)^2 - a^2 over dx gives 2a + dx; st yields 2a). The method simplifies many limit computations by replacing ε–δ with infinitesimal algebra.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chain rule in nonstandard form
rubrics_metrics.description: If G'(a) and F'(G(a)) exist then (F ◦ G)'(a) exists and equals F'(G(a)) · G'(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses infinitesimal increments: let dx be nonzero infinitesimal, set dG = ∗G(a+dx) − G(a), dF = ∗F(G(a)+dG) − F(G(a)), then dF/dx = (dF/dG)·(dG/dx) and take standard parts. This demonstrates how standard calculus theorems can be proved via nonstandard arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language and preliminaries for number theory (start of Chapter 3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define the language of number theory with symbols ∀, 0, S, <, +, ·, E, and intended structure N = (N; 0, S, <, +, ·, E). Numerals Sk0 denote natural numbers. Preview questions for each reduct: decidability and axiomatization; which subsets of N are definable; structure of nonstandard models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This sets up the program to study decidability/undecidability by showing a fragment of number theory capable of representing computation; the presence of numerals and arithmetic symbols is emphasized as allowing definability of many familiar sets (e.g., primes) and enabling later diagonal/undecidability arguments.
